Trying to Conceive

Congenital uterine shapes: understanding scans and care

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A report describing an unusual uterine shape can leave several different questions tangled together: what developed differently, whether it explains symptoms, and whether anything needs treatment. These questions deserve separate answers. The cavity inside the uterus and its outer outline both matter. A careful description is more useful than assuming that every “divided womb” has the same implications.

Development before birth can leave different patterns

The uterus forms during fetal life from paired structures called Müllerian ducts. Their growth, joining and the formation of a single cavity create several opportunities for anatomical variation. Differences can involve the uterus alone or occur alongside changes in the cervix or vagina. Congenital means present from birth; it does not automatically establish an inherited condition.

The cause is often uncertain, and a new diagnosis is not evidence that you or your parent did something wrong. Historical exposure before birth to the medicine DES is one recognised association with reproductive-tract differences, but it did not affect every exposed child in the same way. Tell your clinician about known exposure; most assessments begin with the anatomy and history rather than an assumed cause.

Septate and bicornuate describe different structures

In a septate uterus, a band of tissue divides the cavity partly or extensively while the external outline is broadly usual. The partition can contain muscle as well as connective tissue. It may extend towards the cervix, and associated cervical or vaginal differences need their own description. A vaginal partition is not interchangeable with a uterine septum.

A bicornuate uterus has a significant indentation on the outside of its upper surface, producing two more distinct upper portions or “horns”. The cavity can also look divided, which is why a picture of the cavity alone may confuse it with a septum. Cutting an internal septum and reconstructing a uterus with an external division are different operations with different evidence.

An arcuate label is usually a minor contour variation

An arcuate uterus has a broad inward curve at the top of the cavity. In the ASRM classification it is regarded as a variation without the clinical significance of a septum. A report using this term should not, on its own, be treated as a reason for an operation or an explanation for a pregnancy loss.

Classification systems use different measurements and names. For example, “bicorporeal” describes a group with an external division in another system. Ask which system was used, whether the images show both contours, and whether an experienced reviewer agrees with the diagnosis. Comparing a single millimetre measurement with an online chart cannot settle a borderline finding.

Didelphys and a hemi-uterus need precise names

Uterus didelphys means two uterine bodies formed separately. The cervices and vagina may also have differences, so “two wombs” is an incomplete description. Pregnancy can be possible; the detailed monitoring and birth questions are covered in our existing guide: https://bemamas.com/pregnancy/double-uterus-and-pregnancy/

A unicornuate uterus, or hemi-uterus, develops mainly on one side. A smaller remnant called a rudimentary horn may have functioning lining and may or may not drain. That distinction matters for pain and treatment. For the specific horn and pregnancy pathway, see https://bemamas.com/trying-to-conceive/unicornuate-uterus-fertility-pregnancy-care/

An absent or underdeveloped uterus needs a different assessment

Some people are born with an absent or incompletely developed uterus and part of the vagina. MRKH syndrome is one explanation; ovaries commonly function and puberty may otherwise progress typically, with absent periods bringing the difference to attention. This is not the same finding as a small cavity, a septum or a uterus tilted backwards.

A specialist should confirm what is present and consider other explanations for absent periods or an apparently absent uterus. Selected hormone or chromosome tests and assessment of associated anatomy can help. Emotional support, privacy and a careful discussion of future choices belong in care. This diagnosis should not be reduced to a scan label or a rushed recommendation for reconstruction.

Symptoms guide assessment but cannot identify the shape

Many uterine differences cause no symptoms and are discovered during imaging for another reason. Others become relevant during assessment of painful periods, difficulty conceiving or pregnancy loss. Recurring pain with little menstrual flow can raise a question about blocked drainage, but ordinary-looking periods do not exclude every associated obstruction.

Keep a short account of periods, pain, previous pregnancies and earlier procedures. Ask for assessment of persistent symptoms rather than assuming an anatomical finding explains everything. If the concern involves a vaginal partition, the separate guide explains that assessment: https://bemamas.com/family-health/vaginal-septum-longitudinal-transverse-diagnosis-care/

Imaging should show the cavity and the outside

Three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound, with or without saline when appropriate, is the ASRM first-line method for evaluating uterine shape. An initial two-dimensional scan may suggest a difference. MRI can clarify complex or uncertain findings. Discuss a suitable approach if an internal scan is not appropriate or acceptable; consent and comfort matter throughout assessment.

A dye X-ray of the uterus and tubes, called HSG, or a camera examination inside the cavity, called hysteroscopy, can answer useful questions but cannot alone show the external contour needed to distinguish some shapes. Neither MRI nor an operation is compulsory for everyone. Tell the team if pregnancy is possible before any planned saline, dye or intrauterine procedure.

Ask which associated structures need checking

The report may need to describe the number and appearance of cavities and cervices, any vaginal partition, and whether a remnant has a lining or an outlet. Kidney and urinary-tract differences sometimes accompany these developmental patterns. Mapping the anatomy before treatment helps avoid applying the right procedure to the wrong structure.

Kidney imaging is particularly important with Müllerian agenesis or a one-sided obstructed uterine or vaginal pattern. It is not an automatic requirement for an otherwise isolated uterine septum under ASRM guidance. Ask what findings make it useful in your case rather than expecting the same investigation panel for every uterine label.

Septum surgery is a decision with uncertain benefits

Hysteroscopic septum incision uses instruments through the cervix to divide an internal partition. ASRM guidance supports offering it after recurrent miscarriage through shared decision-making; its benefit for infertility alone is uncertain. RANZCOG’s 2025 guideline conditionally recommends against septum resection, while allowing individual consideration of benefits and harms. The difference reflects uncertainty in the evidence, not a guaranteed answer in either direction.

The small randomised trial discussed in these guidelines did not demonstrate a live-birth benefit, while observational studies have suggested some improvements. Ask which outcome a proposed operation might change and how the evidence fits your history. Discuss bleeding, perforation, scarring, follow-up and the option of observation. An incidental septum before any attempt at pregnancy is not an automatic indication for surgery.

Other treatment and pregnancy plans depend on the findings

Surgery to reshape a bicornuate or double uterus is generally not routine because evidence of benefit is limited and the operation has risks. Treating obstructed menstrual drainage or a problematic functioning horn is a different clinical question. If a procedure is proposed, ask exactly what it targets and how it could affect future reproductive function.

A healthy pregnancy is possible with many uterine patterns. Some are associated with miscarriage, earlier birth, growth concerns or a baby remaining in a non-head-down position, but a label does not predict an individual outcome. Discuss monitoring and birth planning with the maternity team; the uterine shape alone does not mean everyone needs a caesarean.

Leave with a clear explanation and a plan for new symptoms

Ask for the actual report and a simple explanation of the cavity, outer contour and any associated findings. Clarify what is established, what remains uncertain, whether another scan would change care, and what follow-up is appropriate if you choose observation. A second specialist interpretation can be helpful when reports disagree or irreversible treatment is being considered.

New pelvic pain with possible pregnancy, fever, unusual discharge or difficulty passing urine needs urgent assessment. Seek emergency care for severe or worsening pain, pain with fainting or shoulder-tip pain, or heavy bleeding. Any bleeding in a known pregnancy needs urgent maternity advice, even without pain. Do not assume a known uterine difference explains a new urgent symptom.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask whether the images show both uterine contours and whether the diagnosis changes treatment.

Discuss the exact target and evidence before surgery, including differing septum recommendations and the option of observation.

Arrange individual follow-up for symptoms or pregnancy plans, with urgent assessment for new warning signs.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep scan terminology, previous pregnancy details and questions together for appointments. It cannot classify a uterus from symptoms or images, establish why a pregnancy ended, or decide whether an operation is appropriate.

When to seek help

Urgent assessment is needed for pelvic pain with possible pregnancy, fever, unusual discharge or difficulty urinating. Severe or worsening pain, fainting, shoulder-tip pain with pelvic pain, or heavy bleeding needs emergency care. Any bleeding during a known pregnancy needs urgent maternity advice. New symptoms should not be assumed to come from a known anatomical difference.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The internal cavity and external outline distinguish uterine patterns that may look similar on one view.
  • A septum, two uterine bodies, a hemi-uterus and an absent uterus raise different questions.
  • Use specialist imaging and selective associated-anatomy checks before considering treatment.
  • Guidelines differ on septum surgery; benefit, uncertainty and procedural risks need discussion.
  • Many people have successful pregnancies, with care based on their findings and history.

Frequently asked questions

How are congenital uterine differences diagnosed?

Imaging needs to clarify both the cavity and external shape. Three-dimensional ultrasound is often the first detailed assessment; selected MRI can resolve complex or uncertain anatomy. A cavity-only test cannot distinguish every pattern.

Can someone with two uteruses become pregnant?

Yes. Uterus didelphys does not rule out conception or a healthy pregnancy. Associated cervical or vaginal findings and previous pregnancies help determine monitoring and birth plans; neither surgery nor caesarean birth is automatic.

Can pregnancy happen with a unicornuate uterus?

Yes, but the main cavity and any rudimentary horn need specific assessment. A functioning horn can raise separate pain or pregnancy concerns. Use the linked guide for this pattern and arrange specialist advice rather than applying information about a septum.

Can a uterine septum be treated?

It can be divided hysteroscopically in selected circumstances. Whether that improves the outcome you want is less certain. Guidelines differ, so discuss your pregnancy history, possible benefit, surgical risks and observation before deciding.

Does an arcuate uterus need correction?

Usually an arcuate contour is treated as a minor variation rather than a surgical target. If the report is borderline or conflicting, ask how the finding was classified before attributing symptoms or pregnancy loss to it.

Does an absent uterus mean the ovaries are absent too?

Not necessarily. In MRKH, ovaries commonly function despite an absent or underdeveloped uterus. Specialist assessment confirms the diagnosis, checks associated findings and offers support; different causes of absent periods require different care.

Must everyone have their kidneys scanned?

No single rule fits all patterns. Agenesis and one-sided obstruction particularly justify renal assessment. ASRM does not recommend routine kidney investigation for an isolated uterine septum; ask what your complete findings indicate.

Should an unexpected finding be operated on before trying for pregnancy?

An operation is not automatic. First confirm the anatomy, symptoms and reproductive history. Evidence does not establish a benefit from routinely treating an incidental septum before conception has been attempted, and other shapes have different treatment considerations.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
